title: White House AI Task Force Urges 12 Months of Liability Relief for Companies That Report AI-Linked Cyber Incidents
dek: The task force told federal agencies to limit regulatory penalties for good-faith voluntary reports of cyber vulnerabilities and incidents, arguing that AI-fueled attacks have made old standards outdated.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: The North Portico of the White House in Washington, D.C.

keyPoints: The White House AI task force said on Nov. 12 that agencies should limit regulatory liability for good-faith voluntary reporting of cyber vulnerabilities and incidents.
The recommended relief should last at least 12 months, with the possibility of extension, according to the task force statement.
The task force said prior enforcement standards may be outdated because AI is changing the cyber threat environment.
The statement is a recommendation to agencies. It does not itself change any law or rule, and CISA's incident-reporting rule is still forthcoming.
body:
## What the task force recommended

The White House AI task force told federal agencies on Thursday, Nov. 12, that they should limit regulatory liability for companies that voluntarily report cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents. In a statement after its second meeting, the group said “prior standards for taking regulatory action against organizations in response to cyber incidents may be outdated,” and asked agencies to “implement limitations on regulatory liability for good-faith voluntary reporting” when doing so is “lawful, practical, and consistent with the interests of the American people, including public health and safety” ([Cybersecurity Dive](https://cybersecuritydive.com/news/ai-white-house-task-force-cybersecurity-regulation/874679)).

The flexibility should last “for at least the next 12 months,” with the possibility of extension based on an ongoing review of the risk landscape, the statement said, according to Cybersecurity Dive. Bloomberg reported the same recommendation from the meeting, citing an administration official ([Bloomberg](https://bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-14/white-house-urges-easing-liability-to-encourage-ai-disclosure)).

## Why the task force says the rules need to change

The group argued that the risk has moved. “It is clear that the cybersecurity risk environment has changed and organizations that only a short time ago had reasonable protections in place are now more vulnerable,” the statement said. It framed the concern as a chilling effect: older enforcement standards could discourage the information sharing the government needs during a fast-moving threat.

The meeting also covered work with frontier AI labs. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross described efforts to identify and reduce security risks in new AI models, and the National Security Agency and the National Institute of Standards and Technology have been testing frontier models with major labs, according to Cybersecurity Dive. Cairncross and Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s top research official, discussed a process for companies to voluntarily report AI-related incidents. Under that framework, the government would analyze reports and share findings with the private sector.

## Disclosure, not penalties

Bloomberg’s framing is that the change is meant to get AI developers to disclose more. The task force’s own language is about voluntary reporting. It said the goal was to remove requirements that could “have a chilling effect on reporting and information sharing at a time when reporting is critical.” The group said good-faith disclosures should not expose companies to “punitive regulatory or administrative action or civil liability” in the group’s wording.

## What the recommendation does not do

The statement is advice to agencies. It does not create a safe harbor by itself. The task force also said it supports the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s forthcoming incident-reporting rule, and hopes it sets “clear and practical reporting requirements that minimize duplication.” Cybersecurity Dive noted that the rule could add complexity for companies already facing overlapping cyber regulations. The group also backed long-term reauthorization of the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, which it described as soon to expire.

## Market and sector angle

For now the direct effect is on policy, not earnings. Companies that build or deploy frontier AI models could benefit if reporting incidents carries less legal exposure, which may encourage fuller disclosure. Public companies that sell security tools or run AI infrastructure would also be affected by any final rule. The recommendation is not a rule, and no company has been named in it.

## Sourcing

The quotations from the task force statement come from Cybersecurity Dive’s report on it, and the account of the meeting comes from Bloomberg’s reporting. CASRAI’s coverage dates the recommendation to Nov. 12, the day of the meeting. An official White House or OSTP text of the statement was not among the sources reviewed for this story, so the wording here is as reported.
